transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-13
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood CSM); Alan Rivers (Brinewell VP Eng), Serena Kwan (SRE), Tom Brooks (Security), Hannah Li (Data Eng)

Summary:
Short kickoff to align activation plan for Brinewell Energy's inference migration. Main topics: network/VPC model, deployment mode (Dedicated vs Private), benchmark plan, security/compliance checklist, and next-step owner assignments.

Topics:
- Goals & success criteria
- Current architecture & constraints
- Deployment options and tradeoffs
- Observability and runbook expectations
- Pilot timeline and acceptance criteria

ACTION (quick recap at end): Redwood to send runbook & checklist; SE benchmark; customer to provide prompts + compliance contacts.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood. Um, quick intros — we'll go around in one pass. Diego I'll, I'll let you do quick intro after I —
[00:11] Alan Rivers: Hey all, Alan Rivers, VP Eng at Brinewell. We're looking to move inference out of our experimental cluster into something more predictable, less fire-fighty.
[00:19] Serena Kwan: Serena here, SRE, I own the infra side and the VPC peering/network stuff.
[00:24] Tom Brooks: Tom Brooks, security. I'll be doing the questionnaire and internal review.
[00:28] Hannah Li: Hannah, data eng, will own the prompt sets and ops integration.
[00:32] Diego Alvarez: Diego, Redwood solutions engineer — I'll lead benchmarks and integrations.
[00:36] Priya Nair: Priya, CSM, here to coordinate timelines and runbook handoffs.
[00:41] Maya Chen: Great. Alan, can you kick off with the primary goals and any hard constraints?

[01:00] Alan Rivers: Sure. High level — we need a stable inference endpoint for summarization and classification in production by end of Q3. Current things are running on our on-prem GPU fleet, and it's just not predictable. Two big constraints: data must not leave our VPC for regulatory reasons for certain workloads, and cost needs to be below our current N1 per-token cost ideally. Also latency SLO is 300ms p95 for single-shot summarization.

[01:38] Maya Chen: Okay so two constraints: VPC/private deployments for regulated data, cost target, and 300ms p95. Good. Um, Diego, thoughts on how we usually approach that?

[01:51] Diego Alvarez: Yeah. So there are a couple of common paths we recommend — hosted for quick get-go, dedicated reserved capacity for predictable throughput, and private (VPC or on-prem) for strict residency. For Brinewell given the VPC requirement, looks like Private or Dedicated in a VPC mode. We often do a pilot on Redwood Dedicated + VPC peering, so the customer keeps control of network path.

[02:20] Serena Kwan: Quick Q: by Dedicated + VPC peering, do you mean Redwood-owned GPUs in a network that we peer to, or will traffic route over public internet?

[02:31] Diego Alvarez: Good question — with dedicated you get reserved GPU pools and we can set up private connectivity (VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink) so traffic doesn't traverse the public internet. There is a small amount of control plane traffic, but data paths for inference tokens can be configured to stay within your VPC via secure tunnels.

[02:54] Tom Brooks: What about key management? We can't hand over raw keys. We need KMS integration (customer-managed keys) and audit logs that show model access. Also SOC2 attestation.

[03:08] Maya Chen: Totally. We support KMS integrations and customer-managed keys for Private deployments; for Dedicated we can integrate with your KMS via a customer-managed encryption key flow. We'll also provide audit logs and model-level access traces. We'll include the SOC2 and network diagram in the package.

[03:30] Alan Rivers: Good. Can you give us a rough breakdown of cost levers — like quantization, batching, and caching — and how that'll affect latency? We don't want a big regress on the 300ms p95.

[03:45] Diego Alvarez: Yeah, so tradeoffs: quantization reduces cost but might impact latency mildly for some ops, especially in warm KV-cached workloads. We do prefix/KV caching and continuous batching heuristics that lower per-token cost and usually *improve* effective latency for amortized workloads, but for single-shot 300ms p95 we may tune batching close to zero and rely on lower-latency kernels and priority routing. There's also model choice: smaller distilled variants for hot paths.

[04:16] Hannah Li: On the prompts — our live traffic is mostly 1–3 shot summarization with ~800 tokens input and ~120 tokens output. Average request size is ~1k tokens. Throughput is about 15 req/sec in peak, but spikes to 40 for certain campaigns.

[04:33] Diego Alvarez: Helpful — that lets us size GPU pools. If you're at 1k tokens and p95 300ms, we can design a canary with a lower sequence length or a distilled model to meet the SLO then scale to bigger model if quality warrants.

[04:50] Serena Kwan: For the peering, we'll need a runbook and a list of IP ranges, certificates, and firewall rules. Also, what about egress logs for compliance?

[05:03] Priya Nair: We'll share a VPC checklist in the runbook. It includes IP ranges, SA keys, TLS cert expectations, SAML SSO endpoints. On egress logs, Redwood provides connection and audit logs — Diego can confirm retention windows.

[05:21] Diego Alvarez: Retention is configurable; default is 90 days for logs we push, longer with add-on. We can also support pushing logs into your SIEM via secure forwarder.

[05:33] Tom Brooks: We have an internal procurement and security questionnaire — can you commit to a turnaround timeline if we send it this week? 7–10 business days would be ideal.

[05:42] Maya Chen: Yes we can. We aim for 7 business days for basic security questionnaires, longer if there are custom requests. We'll assign our security specialist to own that.

[05:53] Alan Rivers: On integration — we want CI hooks to roll model versions and a canary policy. How do rollouts look?

[06:02] Diego Alvarez: Rollouts are built-in: you can pin versions, do canaries (traffic %), automatic fallback to previous model variants, and A/B testing. We also expose tracing hooks so you can tie evaluation metrics back to prompts.

[06:18] Hannah Li: We'll need the SDKs and examples for our Python microservices — especially how to pass metadata and correlation ids for tracing.

[06:25] Diego Alvarez: We'll provide SDK snippets and the open-source reference template. I'll attach a sample middleware that injects correlation IDs and extracts latency traces.

[06:37] Serena Kwan: About private on-prem option, is there an air-gapped package? Some of our workloads must stay in the datacenter.

[06:45] Maya Chen: Yes, we offer on-prem package for regulated workloads; that typically includes a customer-managed control plane and a runtime that can be deployed inside your datacenter or air-gapped environment. That path has longer lead time for onboarding.

[06:58] Alan Rivers: Which path would you recommend as a fast pilot so we hit early Q3?

[07:05] Diego Alvarez: Fastest is Redwood Dedicated with VPC peering because we can provision a reserved pool and run benchmarks within two weeks. Private on-prem would take longer — typically 4–8 weeks to validate networking and install.

[07:20] Tom Brooks: If we start with Dedicated, can we later transition to on-prem with minimal changes?

[07:27] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we design for portability: model artifacts, config, and rollout policies are portable. Some networking and key management changes required, but operationally it's smooth if planned.

[07:38] Priya Nair: For the pilot acceptance criteria — here's a suggested set: 1) p95 latency <= 300ms for the canary traffic slice; 2) quality thresholds measured against our lab prompts (we'll need Hannah's prompts); 3) audit logs available and accessible. Are those acceptable?

[07:58] Alan Rivers: Yes that's fine. Also want a cost projection for 3 months of expected traffic and a projection under 2x peak.

[08:07] Maya Chen: We'll include cost projections in the runbook. Diego, we'll need the model and GPU sizing to estimate.

[08:14] Diego Alvarez: Understood; I'll build a conservative estimate and a sensitivity table for sequence length and concurrent requests.

[08:22] Serena Kwan: Any specific ports we should open, or do you use established TLS endpoints?

[08:29] Diego Alvarez: We use TLS over standard HTTPS ports for inference endpoints. For peering there may be internal ranges and an option to require mTLS if desired.

[08:40] Hannah Li: About data retention — how long do you keep input prompts and outputs for debugging? We have to ensure PII isn't stored beyond policy.

[08:48] Maya Chen: By default, we retain logs for 90 days. For Private/on-prem, retention is configured by you. We also support auto-scrubbing of PII in logs and an option to disable storing raw inputs entirely. We'll put that in the runbook.

[09:05] Tom Brooks: Good. We'll need to see the PII scrubbing flow and any guarantees. Also, can you support redaction hooks before storage?

[09:13] Diego Alvarez: Yes, there are hooks and a pre-storage filter to remove or hash sensitive fields. We can walk through patterns in the benchmark session.

[09:22] Priya Nair: Logistics — who's the POC for network from your side, Serena? And for prompts Hannah? We'll track these as owners.

[09:31] Serena Kwan: Yep Serena for network.
[09:34] Hannah Li: Hannah for prompts.

[09:37] Maya Chen: Great. OK quick timeline proposal: this week we exchange runbook and sample prompts; next week SE-led benchmark and peering prep; two weeks after benchmark we run a 48–72 hour canary. Does that sound feasible?

[09:52] Alan Rivers: Sounds good. Two quick asks — one: can we get an NDA or addendum for data handling? Two: are there any dependencies on our side that tend to block the peering?

[10:04] Maya Chen: We can push a data processing addendum and/or NDA. Typical blocking items are firewall rules, cert provisioning, and service account creation for the peering. We'll send a checklist.

[10:15] Tom Brooks: On compliance: you'll share SOC2 and any pen test summaries?

[10:19] Maya Chen: Yes. We'll include SOC2 report and a high-level pen test summary; detailed red-team artifacts usually go through our security NDA process.

[10:29] Hannah Li: For the benchmark, can we simulate our 40 req/sec spikes? We want to see autoscale behavior.

[10:35] Diego Alvarez: Absolutely. The test harness will emulate traffic patterns and burst behavior. We'll also test cache warm-up and cold-starts.

[10:43] Serena Kwan: One more: any recommended observability integrations? We run Datadog and Splunk.

[10:50] Diego Alvarez: We have native exporters and can push metrics and traces to Datadog, Splunk, or your own Prometheus. We also export request-level traces for sampling.

[10:59] Priya Nair: Ok I'm going to capture next steps and owners. Maya, Diego, Hannah, Tom — we have action items. Anything else before we recap?

[11:08] Alan Rivers: Just want to reiterate that if latency degrades beyond 300ms p95 we need automatic fallback to a simpler model. That should be part of the canary plan.

[11:17] Diego Alvarez: Agreed — we can configure an automatic fallback and failover policy that routes to a lower-latency model variant or to our cached responses.

[11:25] Tom Brooks: Also confirm SSO — we use Okta and will want SAML.

[11:29] Maya Chen: Okta via SAML is supported; we'll share SAML setup doc.

[11:35] Priya Nair: Recap and owners: Maya to send runbook + SOC2 + DPA addendum; Diego to send benchmark plan & test harness; Hannah to share sample prompts; Tom to run internal security questionnaire and send to us. We'll aim to reconvene after Diego's benchmark results.

[11:55] Alan Rivers: Thanks everyone. We'll look for materials and schedule the bench next week.

[11:59] Maya Chen: Thanks — I'll follow up with links and schedule invites.

[12:05] (call ends)
